why: A single-page app changes the screen by asking its ROUTER, not by asking the server. `router.push('/auth/login')` swaps the component the browser is already showing; no request leaves the machine. Read as an HTTP call it becomes a route nothing serves, and in a multi-service pack such a false call can even try to cross into a sibling project. So the navigation sinks are declared here, per router, the same way the HTTP clients are declared in http-clients.json: a call on one of these is a screen change, and the web lane records where it goes instead of pretending a request was sent. A server-rendered page is the other case and is left alone: there a link IS a request, and the sink is what tells the two apart, not the file kind.

routers.why: `this.$router` is the router the framework itself puts on every component, so its name is part of Vue's own vocabulary rather than a habit of one project. The composition form binds the same object to a name of its own, which is what `hooks` covers.
`useNavigate()` hands back the navigate FUNCTION itself, so the call is on the name the hook was assigned to and there is no method to name. `redirect(...)` is the same act written as an import.

elements.why: A `<router-link>` is written in a single-file component's `<template>`, and this worker parses a component's `<script>` blocks and not its markup. The sink is declared here because it is one; it is not reached yet, and docs/setup/web-lane.md says so rather than leaving a reader to find out.

globals.why: The address bar is on `window`, so no file imports it and nothing binds it. Setting `href` or calling `assign` / `replace` on it opens another page: it is the browser doing the navigating, which is the one thing every one of these routers ends up asking for.
